In brief

Parody. "And at the sound of the sacring bell, headed by a crucifer with acolytes, thurifers, boatbearers, readers, ostiarii, deacons and subdeacons, the blessed company drew nigh of mitred abbots and priors and guardians and monks and friars [...] per Christum Dominum nostrum": after much antisemitic muttering about the recently departed Bloom, Martin Cunningham reminds everyone of their good fortune in having been born into the correct religion. His "God bless here is all my prayer" is seconded by the Citizen's "Amen" and Joe Hynes's "And I'm sure He will." This chauvinistic sentiment is immediately amplified by an immense procession of Catholic clerics, monastics, teachers, saints, and martyrs, marching in their thousands up to the door of Barney Kiernan's to consecrate it as a holy place with miracles and prophecies and clouds of incense and sprinklings of holy water and invocations of the biblical patriarchs. The celebrant leading the ceremony enters the pub to sanctify its offerings, performing a handy all-purpose blessing that the church has written for non-liturgical occasions. The parody, then, fulfills Cunningham's prayer in the most literal and the most extravagant way possible.

At more length

The blessing begins with the ringing of the "sacring bell," also known as a sanctus bell or altar bell, that Stephen thought of in Proteus as he contemplated priests handling the consecrated Host. Here it marks the arrival of an immense procession such as one might see streaming through the streets of Rome and the Vatican on a high holy day, but phantasmagorically heightened. It is led by "a crucifer" (in Latin, literally "cross-bearer") carrying a large cross, and behind him "acolytes, thurifers, boatbearers, readers, ostiarii, deacons and subdeacons"—men carrying incense holders ("thuribles" and "boats"), men who read scriptural passages ("lessons") during church services, ushers or doorkeepers (from Latin ostium = door), and lesser ordained ministers who assist the celebrant during Mass. After them come "abbots and priors and guardians and monks and friars"—the unordained members of various religious orders and the rulers of their houses, listed in encyclopedic detail.

"And after came all saints and martyrs, virgins and confessors," detailed no less exhaustively. All these thousands of men and women, it may be noted, are dead (though eternally present to the faithful). One of the martyred saints, Ursula, is accompanied by "eleven thousand virgins," themselves all martyred. The identifying symbolic objects that the saints carry give Joyce another opportunity for encyclopedic cataloguing, with some dips into bathos ("babes in a bathtub," "buckshot," "boxes of vaseline"). The saints' documented facility at performing miracles provides another such opportunity, with its own mixture of the Christlike sublime ("raising the dead to life") and the bathetically mundane ("discovering various articles which had been mislaid"). Two sacred musical numbers add to the synesthetic overload. At the end of the procession three figures walk "beneath a canopy of cloth of gold"—a feature seen in images displayed here.

When the procession reaches the pub, "the celebrant blessed the house and censed the mullioned windows and the groynes and the vaults and the arrises and the capitals and the pediments and the cornices and the engrailed arches and the spires and the cupolas and sprinkled the lintels thereof with blessed water." These ceremonial actions that a priest might perform in consecrating a mighty stone church are absurdly inapplicable to the mean pub on Little Britain Street. The priest then prays that "God might bless that house as he had blessed the house of Abraham and Isaac and Jacob and make the angels of His light to inhabit therein. And entering he blessed the viands and the beverages." The first sentence, Gifford notes, very closely echoes a "Blessing for a House" that is no longer included in Catholic ritual. The second one recalls the Benedictio Panis, Vini, Aquae et Fructum ("blessing of bread, wine, water, and fruits"), which is still used.

The verbal blessings conclude with more Latin, first a responsory formula that precedes formal prayers in the Catholic church: "Adiutorium nostrum in nomine Domini. / Qui fecit coelum et terram. / Dominus vobiscum. / Et cum spiritu tuo" ("Our help is in the name of the Lord. / Who made heaven and earth. / The Lord be with you. / And with your spirit"), and then the end of the Benedictio ad Omnia ("blessing to all"), an all-purpose prayer devised for non-liturgical settings, because Barney Kiernan's is not, after all, a church: "Deus, cuius verbo sanctificantur omnia, benedictionem tuam effunde super creaturas istas: et praesta ut quisquis eis secundum legem et voluntatem Tuam cum gratiarum actione usus fuerit per invocationem sanctissimi nominis Tui corporis sanitatem et animae tutelam Te auctore percipiat per Christum Dominum nostrum" ("God, by whose word all things are sanctified, pour down your blessing on these creations of yours: and grant that whoever has used them gratefully, following your law and will, may, through the invocation of your most holy name, you being his maker, gain health of body and protection of soul, through Christ our Lord").

No one in the bar would understand these words: Latin is for priests, not parishioners. But they would certainly welcome the message. Both benedictions bless the ale being consumed in the pub, and the second one prays that all who consume it in the proper spirit may be rewarded with bodily health and mental fortitude. Joyce's ironies are seldom more pointed. The men guzzling beer and demeaning Jews in Barney Kiernan's may not seem very christian, but the parody confirms their conviction that God and all his saints above approve of them just as they are. As for poor Bloom, it seems that all of holy Christendom has showed up to repudiate him.

John Hunt 2026
